source: OECD (2025), Health at a Glance 2025: OECD Indicators, OECD Publishing, Paris
framing: Gap framing: every figure is what is NOT covered, NOT satisfied or unmet. Gap figures are 100 minus the published figure.
rule: HAL may phrase these facts freely but must not state any figure, ranking or claim that is not in this list. Verbatim report sentences may name other countries; only what they say about this country may be used.

facts.text: 38% of people in Iceland were NOT satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live in 2024, versus an OECD average of 36%; satisfaction has deteriorated over the past decade.
16.4% of health spending in Iceland was NOT covered by government or compulsory insurance schemes in 2023, versus an OECD average of 24.9%.
2.8% of people in Iceland reported unmet medical care needs due to cost, distance or waiting times in 2024 (average of 28 OECD countries: 3.4%).
1% of hospital care costs in Iceland were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 11% on average in the OECD.
16% of outpatient medical care costs in Iceland were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 22% on average in the OECD.
66% of dental care costs in Iceland were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 68% on average in the OECD.
59% of pharmaceutical costs in Iceland were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 42% on average in the OECD.
More than 8% of people in Greece, Latvia and Iceland reported unmet dental care needs in 2024, compared to fewer than 1% in Germany, Hungary and the Netherlands, as well as accession country Croatia.

In many countries, patients have access to free acute inpatient care or only need to make a small copayment; as a result, coverage rates were near 100% in Sweden, Norway, Iceland and Estonia, as well as accession country Romania.

Figure 6.12 reveals broad consistency in the proportion of patients with diabetes on recommended antihypertensive medications in 2023, although Iceland, the Netherlands and Türkiye had rates at around 80% or lower.
Iceland, Portugal, Italy, Korea and Sweden reported rates lower than 12 per 100 000 population, while Chile, Czechia, Slovenia and Germany reported rates higher than 40 per 100 000.

Confidence in self-management among people aged 45 and over with chronic conditions varied almost four-fold across surveyed countries, ranging from 92% in France to under 40% in Italy, Iceland and Greece.
The same set of healthcare items costs 55% more than the OECD average in Iceland, and 52% more in Switzerland and the United States – the countries reporting the highest prices.
Central, regional or local government schemes in Sweden, Norway, Iceland, Denmark and the United Kingdom accounted for 80% or more of national health spending.

With public health emergency measures phased out after the acute phase of the pandemic, the share of preventive spending dropped and reached pre-pandemic levels by 2023, ranging from 6-7% of total health spending in Canada and the United Kingdom to less than 3% in Poland, Belgium, Iceland, France, Switzerland, Portugal and Japan.
